stories.headline: ECONOMY UNEXPECTEDLY SHEDS 23,000 JOBS IN JULY, STOCKS RALLY TO A RECORD ON RATE-CUT HOPES
stories.body: Nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 versus a forecast gain of 83,000, and May-June figures were revised down a combined 103,000, even as the unemployment rate held at 4.1% and labor-force participation slid to 61.4%, its lowest in more than five years. The S&P 500 rose 0.62% to a record 7,757.64 as traders priced in higher odds of a September Fed rate cut.
stories.explain: A payrolls miss this large shifts the market's estimate of the Fed's reaction function almost instantly, because fed funds futures reprice the odds of a September cut within minutes of the release. Lower expected short-term rates flow through a discounted-cash-flow model as a lower discount rate on future corporate earnings, which mechanically raises today's fair value for equities even though nothing about the earnings themselves has changed. The falling participation rate is the nuance to watch — it suggests some of today's weakness is workers exiting the labor force rather than pure layoffs, a subtly different signal for the Fed than demand destruction.

stories.headline: 2-YEAR YIELD SINKS 5 BPS TO 4.19% AS TRADERS RAMP UP BETS ON A SEPTEMBER FED CUT
stories.body: The policy-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield fell as much as 9 bps intraday to touch 4.15% before settling near 4.19%, its lowest level since July 17, while the 10-year fell a smaller 3 bps to 4.65% — a curve-steepening move typical of a market pricing in near-term easing.
stories.explain: The 2-year yield moves more than the 10-year on a weak jobs report because it's most directly anchored to where the Fed funds rate will sit over the next two years, while the 10-year also embeds long-run growth and inflation expectations that are stickier. When short rates fall faster than long rates, the yield curve steepens — exactly what happened today — and that steepening is itself a market signal that investors expect the Fed to start cutting rather than merely pause.

stories.headline: S&P 500 CAPS BEST WEEK SINCE APRIL WITH RECORD CLOSE, NASDAQ 100 ADDS ROUGHLY 1%
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,757.64 and the Dow added 138 points, or 0.3%, while the Nasdaq 100 gained about 1% as tech led the rally on the view that a softer labor market gives the Fed more room to ease.
stories.explain: 'Bad news is good news' only holds when the market believes the economy is weakening gradually enough that the Fed can offset it with rate cuts before it becomes a genuine growth scare — investors are betting on the soft-landing interpretation of today's data rather than a recession signal. That's a real gamble: if next week's data confirms broader deterioration rather than a one-off payrolls miss, the same rate-cut logic that lifted stocks today can flip into a growth-scare selloff instead.

stories.headline: GOLD JUMPS 2.6% TOWARD $4,357 AS SOFT JOBS DATA AND HORMUZ TENSIONS PULL IN THE SAME DIRECTION
stories.body: Gold climbed 2.6% to roughly $4,357 an ounce, boosted by falling Treasury yields after the jobs miss, while WTI crude rose about 1% to $78.16 as renewed tension around the Strait of Hormuz kept a geopolitical risk premium in oil.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost falls in lockstep with real interest rates — today's drop in Treasury yields directly lowers the cost of holding non-yielding bullion instead of interest-bearing bonds, which is the main driver of the 2.6% move. It's also catching a bid as a geopolitical hedge against the Hormuz situation, meaning gold is rallying on both a rate story and a risk story simultaneously, which is why it's outperforming nearly every other asset class today.

stories.headline: NCAA WARNS COACHES OF MID-SEASON SUSPENSIONS AS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS RESHAPE THE TRANSFER PORTAL
stories.body: The NCAA told member schools it will suspend any coach for half a season if their roster includes a player later ruled ineligible, a response to a wave of eligibility lawsuits. Gonzaga added Florida State transfer Chauncey Wiggins, and Houston landed Texas transfer Chendall Weaver after a Tennessee judge ruled him eligible for a fifth season.

stories.headline: KINGS WAIVE SIX-TIME ALL-STAR DEMAR DEROZAN, INSTANTLY ONE OF THE TOP NAMES LEFT IN FREE AGENCY
stories.body: Sacramento waived DeMar DeRozan, making the six-time All-Star an unrestricted free agent; the Wizards have already opened talks with him. Elsewhere, the Clippers-Raptors trade sending Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto remains on hold pending the NBA's investigation into alleged impermissible benefits.

stories.headline: PRESEASON KICKS OFF AS RUNNING BACK MARKET RESETS WITH BIJAN ROBINSON, JAHMYR GIBBS, JONATHAN TAYLOR EXTENSIONS
stories.body: The Panthers and Cardinals played the league's first live preseason snaps of 2026 following Thursday's Hall of Fame Game, while a run of extensions for top backs Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs and Jonathan Taylor reset the position's pay scale. All 32 teams remain in training camp ahead of Week 1 of the preseason.

stories.headline: PROPOSED COLLEGE SPORTS BILL AMENDMENT COULD TRIGGER A NEW WAVE OF CONFERENCE REALIGNMENT
stories.body: A proposed amendment to a pending college sports bill in Congress could reopen conference realignment just as the sport settles into its current power-conference structure, with the 2026 season kicking off Aug. 29. Preseason All-America teams were also released this week.

deepDive.title: Why a Weak Jobs Report Sent Stocks to a Record: Inside the Fed's Reaction Function
content: Today's setup looks paradoxical on its face: the U.S. economy just lost 23,000 jobs when Wall Street expected a gain of 83,000, one of the ugliest payrolls misses in recent memory, and the S&P 500 responded by closing at a record high. That's not the market ignoring bad news — it's the market repricing what bad economic news means for Fed policy. Understanding why requires separating two questions that get conflated in headlines: is the economy doing well, and is monetary policy about to get easier? Today, the answer to the first question was clearly no, but the answer to the second question moved sharply toward yes, and for equities right now, the second question matters more.

The mechanism runs through the Fed's reaction function — the market's model of how the central bank responds to incoming data. A payrolls miss this large, compounded by 103,000 in downward revisions to the prior two months, immediately raises the probability traders assign to a September rate cut, which shows up within minutes in fed funds futures pricing. That expected path of future short-term rates is the discount rate used to value every future dollar of corporate earnings. Lower the discount rate and the present value of those future earnings rises mechanically, even though nothing about the earnings themselves has changed. That is why the 2-year Treasury yield, which tracks near-term Fed expectations most closely, fell 5 bps to 4.19% while the 10-year fell a smaller 3 bps — the curve steepened because the move was concentrated in what the Fed does over the next two years, not what happens to growth over the next decade.

What most casual market-watchers miss is that this trade only works as long as investors believe the labor market is cooling gradually rather than falling apart. The Fed's dual mandate means it wants labor demand to soften just enough to keep inflation contained without tipping into a genuine downturn — the soft-landing scenario. A useful historical parallel is September 2024, when the Fed cut rates 50 bps on the back of a similarly soft jobs report and equities rallied on the same logic. But the tell inside today's data is the participation rate, which fell to 61.4%, its lowest in over five years. A falling participation rate can mean workers are giving up on job searches rather than being laid off, a subtly different and arguably more concerning signal than straightforward demand weakness, since it does not reverse as quickly when conditions improve.

That distinction is exactly what next week's CPI report on Wednesday will help resolve. If inflation data comes in soft alongside continued labor weakness, the market's current bet — that this is the start of an easing cycle rather than the leading edge of a growth scare — gets validated, and today's record close holds. If CPI surprises to the upside, the Fed faces the classic bind of a softening labor market colliding with sticky inflation, and the same rate-cut logic that lifted stocks today would need to unwind fast. That is the trade to watch heading into next week: not whether the data is good or bad in isolation, but whether it stays internally consistent with the soft-landing story the market just paid a record price to believe.
